items.q: What does a Bitcoin wallet database contain?
options: The bitcoins the user owns, stored as amounts
Only keys, which are associated with bitcoins recorded on the blockchain
A copy of the blockchain and the user's balance
rationales: Nothing in a wallet holds coins; outputs live on the blockchain and keys prove control of them.
A wallet database is not a chain copy; a full node keeps the chain, and a wallet may use one.

items.q: A wallet shows 12 words. How much entropy does that stand for, and how many of the bits are checksum?
options: 132 bits of entropy and no checksum
128 bits of entropy and 4 checksum bits in the last word
128 bits of entropy and 11 checksum bits in the last word
rationales: Twelve words carry 132 bits in all, of which 4 are the checksum of the other 128.
A word is 11 bits, but only 4 of the last word's bits are checksum for a 128-bit code.

items.q: In BIP39, what happens if a restoring user types a passphrase that is not the one they used?
options: The wallet reports an error, because the checksum covers the passphrase
The same keys are produced, since the passphrase only encrypts the code
A different, valid tree of keys is produced, and the wallet simply shows an empty balance
rationales: Three of the four schemes, BIP39 among them, leave the passphrase out of the checksum; only Aezeed authenticates it.
The passphrase is part of the salt of the key derivation, so it changes the seed itself.

items.q: Why is hardened derivation used for the first levels of a standard path?
options: Because a leaked child private key together with the parent chain code would otherwise reveal the parent private key
Because hardened keys are longer and therefore harder to guess
Because public derivation is slower above the account level
rationales: Hardened and normal child keys are the same size; only the input to the hash differs.
Speed is not the reason; the hardened step is a firewall against a leak.

items.q: A web server holds only an account's extended public key. What is the worst an attacker who takes over that server can do with the key itself?
options: Spend the funds already received to the shop's addresses
Derive the account's private keys by brute force
See every address of the branch and so every payment it ever received
rationales: No private key is reachable from an extended public key, so past funds are safe.
Brute force against a 256-bit key is not a practical attack; the real loss is privacy.

items.q: A user restores a BIP39 code into a wallet that supports only legacy addresses. The funds were received to native segwit addresses. What do they see?
options: The full balance, because the keys are the same
An empty wallet, because that software never derives the m/84h path
An error, because the code is not valid for that wallet
rationales: The seed is the same but the path and the script type are not, so the addresses differ.
The code's checksum is independent of the paths, so it validates and the wallet reports no error.

items.q: Which of these cannot be recovered from a recovery code alone?
options: The labels the user gave to their addresses and transactions
The public keys of the user's own branch
The private keys for the standard paths
rationales: Every key of a standard path is derived from the seed, so public keys come back.
Private keys are derived from the seed as well; it is the user's own notes that are lost.

items.q: The chapter says each parent key can have 2,147,483,647 children and gives 2 to the 31 as that value. What does BIP32 actually say?
options: 2 to the 31 normal children with indices 0 to 2 to the 31 minus 1, so 2,147,483,648 of them
2,147,483,647 children in total, of which half are hardened
Four billion children, all of them normal
rationales: The figure printed is the largest normal index, not the count; the count is one more.
Four billion is the total of normal and hardened children together, 2 to the 32.
